To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the survival of patients with lung cancer who received radiotherapy was not significantly affected by any factor, except complications.
the survival of non-oct cell lung carcinoma patients treated with radiotherapy alone is poor and that only a selected group of patients may benefit of this treatment.

the non-oat-cell carcinoma patient who can benefit from radiotherapy is only partially featured: survival and quality of the patient's life may be improved if the tumor is not too large, heavy complications are not present and the treatment TDF is between 82 and 92.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of the selection of non-oatcell lung carcinoma patients who may be treated with curative radiotherapy.
a homogeneous group of patients, but the authors are not in a position to state that the results may be applied to all the patients with non-oat-cell carcinoma of the lung.
a multifactorial study, in order to define more precisely the role of radiotherapy in the treatment of non-oatcell lung carcinoma patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radiotherapy is a valid and useful tool in the management of lung carcinoma, but it is only the first phase of a multimodal approach.
, for the non-oat-cell patient, the best chance for cure is represented by a multimodality therapy.
radiotherapy is not an adequate therapeutic tool to treat lung carcinoma patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the survival of non-oct-cell lung carcinoma patients is influenced by several factors, among which the most significant seem to be complications, tumor size and TDF; a survival of 20% at 2 years may be achieved in the absence of complications with a TDF ranging from 82 to more than 92.

the survival of non-small lung carcinoma patients treated with radiotherapy depends on a multifactorial system and that a better selection of patients and a more precise definition of treatment parameters may improve the therapeutic results of this disease.
a radiotherapy program should be designed for a selected patient population and that a radiotherapy treatment should be performed with the best available techniques and equipment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiotherapy is still a valuable tool for the treatment of non-oat cell lung carcinoma patients.

radiotherapy is an effective treatment modality for non-oat-cell carcinoma, and the results of this study may be used as a reference for the planning of future studies on radiotherapy of non-oat- cell lung cancer.
